extracted.intended_audience: writers of horror/speculative short fiction submitting to Strange Horizons (or similar markets)
extracted.subtask_description: A checklist of overused horror-story plots and variants that Strange Horizons editors saw repeatedly in submissions; intended to signal common clichés writers may want to avoid (or at least be aware of) when submitting. The page notes these are examples, not a canonical list of bad stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serial killer or vampire stalks and slays victim(s).
rubrics_metrics.description: Serial killer or vampire stalks and slays victim(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsidiary variants editors encounter include: the tables are turned at the end (e.g., the intended victim turns out to be a vampire or other powerful supernatural creature); the serial killer is insane; the serial killer is under supernatural influence; the serial killer was abused as a child. Note: the list is a snapshot of things seen too often and not every item is necessarily bad; see the site's main fiction guidelines for submission requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person is insane, and kills a lot of people because of it.
rubrics_metrics.description: Person is insane, and kills a lot of people because of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common variants: the insanity is due to supernatural influence; the insane person does property damage instead of killing people. Editors flag over-reliance on 'insanity' explanations as a frequent, often-tractable trope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist sits around for a while.
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonist sits around for a while.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical payoffs editors see: in the end, it turns out the protagonist is dead; or in the end, it turns out the protagonist is a serial killer. The entry criticizes stories that mainly present a passive protagonist and rely on twist endings of this sort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evil creature kills lots of people.
rubrics_metrics.description: Evil creature kills lots of people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent subvariants: in the end the creature escapes to kill again; the creature is disguised as something cute. Editors note these are very common and can become predictable unless handled with originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person sees mysterious things that nobody else can see.
rubrics_metrics.description: Person sees mysterious things that nobody else can see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common variant: the person has unreasonable dread of a Thing nobody else can see; in the end the Thing gets the person after all. The page flags this as a frequently submitted premise that often lacks freshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person has bad dreams; they turn out to be real.
rubrics_metrics.description: Person has bad dreams; they turn out to be real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical endings editors report: in the end, it turns out the person is crazy; or in the end, it turns out someone is drugging the person. These dream-to-reality arcs are common submission patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warnings are ignored, with unfortunate consequences.
rubrics_metrics.description: Warnings are ignored, with unfortunate consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants include: a person is warned to Always Do something but fails to do it and thereby sets Nameless Evil free; a person is warned to Never Do something but does it anyway and thereby sets Nameless Evil free. This motif of 'ignore warning → doom' is noted as overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: A place is haunted or scary.
rubrics_metrics.description: A place is haunted or scary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors caution this is not really a plot—yet they receive many plotless place descriptions where 'a place is scary' is the only point. The note in the original text: '[No, this isn't a plot, but we do receive plotless place descriptions in which this is the only point.]'

rubrics_metrics.name: Child is abused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subvariants editors see: the tables are turned at the end; the abuser is under supernatural influence; a person is targeted by an Evil Thing and in the end the Evil Thing kills the person. The entry signals frequent use of abuse as a plot starter or motivator in submitted stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horrible things happen to person in the end, either as punishment or irony.
rubrics_metrics.description: Horrible things happen to person in the end, either as punishment or irony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants noted: the person is a bad person and gets their comeuppance via unspeakably horrible events (the 'Twilight Zone' plot); person attempts to kill or dispose of spouse and the tables are turned; person isn't such a bad person but unspeakably horrible things happen to them anyway. Editors flag the moralistic/ironic-punishment payoff as common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person wants or wishes for something, and they get it without any trouble, but it results in horrible things happening to them.
rubrics_metrics.description: Person wants or wishes for something, and they get it without any trouble, but it results in horrible things happening to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This caution concerns 'be careful what you wish for' stories that provide an easy wish-fulfillment setup only to punish the wish; editors report seeing this pattern frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapist enters into the thoughts of serial killer in prison, via telepathy or VR. [a.k.a. the Cell plot.]
rubrics_metrics.description: Therapist enters into the thoughts of serial killer in prison, via telepathy or VR. [a.k.a. the Cell plot.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry calls out this specific premise as a recurring submission trope (often labelled the 'Cell' plot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiate into religion discovers that the religion is actually killing/destroying its initiates.
rubrics_metrics.description: Initiate into religion discovers that the religion is actually killing/destroying its initiates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors note this cult/ritual-initiation-reveal as a frequently submitted horror plotline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alien creature lays eggs under the skin of a human.
rubrics_metrics.description: Alien creature lays eggs under the skin of a human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asterisked as a repeatedly-seen body-horror/parasite premise in submissions; editors have encountered it often enough to include it on the list.

rubrics_metrics.name: A kid has an imaginary friend, but the adults don't believe in it; in the end, the imaginary friend turns out to be real and eeeevil.
rubrics_metrics.description: A kid has an imaginary friend, but the adults don't believe in it; in the end, the imaginary friend turns out to be real and eeeevil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entry calls out the 'imaginary friend secretly evil' twist as a common, oft-submitted storyline.

rubrics_metrics.name: There are zombies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The original text notes: '[We have published zombie stories in the past, but very rarely, and at this point any story featuring zombies is an extremely hard sell for us.]' Editors flag zombie stories as particularly saturated and difficult to place.
